sentences.text: 2. We have heard Shri A.N. Mulla, learned AGA for the State/appellant and perused the trial court record.

3. The prosecution story in nutshell, as alleged in the written report, is that the accused-opposite party Karn Singh, who is the permanent resident of village Kuwankheda, Police Station Nanauta, is the brother-in-law of the first informant and is a harden criminal and remains in bad company of the villagers.

It is further alleged that his minor niece and nephew, both aged about 14 years used to live with the accused-opposite party and taking undue advantage of which, Karn Singh by putting his nephew and niece, in fear of death by a country made pistol has been committing rape, upon her niece for the last two weeks.

4. It is further alleged in the FIR that on 25.06.2017, at about 04:00 p.m., her minor niece was all alone in the house and taking advantage of the said situation, the accused-opposite party caught hold of his niece and by putting her under fear of death, by a country made pistol, committed rape upon her.
On raising alarm, her brother Akash reached there and seriously resisted and asked him not to do so.
Karn Singh in a fit of rage started hurling abuses, extended death threats and assaulted them by the butt of the country made pistol, causing injuries on their persons.
5. On raising alarm by both the children, number of villagers reached there and rescued them, who thereafter reached his house and since then are staying with him.

It is further alleged that on 30.06.2017 at about 11:00 a.m. in the morning Karn Singh reached at his house and started hurling abuses and tried to forcefully take away his niece and nephew, however, on raising alarm by the inmates of the house, number of persons reached there and rescued them, the information of which was sent to the police.

6. On the basis of the above stated written report dated 30.06.2017, an FIR was lodged at Police Station Nanauta, registered vide Case Crime No.120 of 2017, under Sections 323, 504, 506, 376 IPC and Section 3/4 of POCSO Act on 30.06.2017 at 08:30 p.m. in the night.

After registration of the FIR, the investigation was handed over to S.I. Arvind Kumar, who recorded the statement of the first informant and reached the place of incident and prepared the site plan and thereafter recorded the statement of the victim and thereafter sent the victim for medical examination.

The victim was medically examined on 01.07.2017 by P.W.3 Dr. Pratibha, who prepared the medical examination report and the supplementary medical report and proved the same as Exts. Ka-4 and Ka-5.
7.
Thereafter, the investigation was transferred to P.W.4 S.S.I. Satish Kumar, who produced the victim before the Magistrate on 17.07.2017, who recorded her statement under Section 164 Cr.P.C.
Thereafter, after collecting the relevant materials and recording the statements of the witnesses, the Investigating Officer submitted the charge-sheet against the accused-opposite party.

sentences.text:
The trial court framed the charges against the accused-opposite party under Section 376(2)(Cha), 323,
504, 506 IPC and Section 6 POCSO Act, which was further modified and charges were framed under Section 323, 504, 506, 376(2)(Cha) IPC and Section 5(Dha)/6 POCSO Act.
The said charges were read out and explained to the accused-opposite party, who abjured the said charges, pleaded not guilty and insisted to be tried.
9. The prosecution, in order to prove the guilt against the accused-opposite party, produced as many as six witnesses.
In addition to it, the prosecution also produced number of documents, which were duly exhibited and proved.
10. After conclusion of the prosecution evidence, incriminating evidence and circumstances were put to the accused-opposite party in his statement under Section 313 Cr.P.C.
The accused-opposite party alleged the prosecution evidence to be false and fabricated.

He categorically stated that victim's maternal uncle had taken a sum of Rs.5,00,00/- from him and on being asked to return the same, there was a quarrel between them and in the backdrop of the said circumstances, the first informant, in league with the minor victim by misleading her, had got a false case registered against him though he is innocent, however, he did not led any defence evidence.

11. The learned trial court after thrashing the evidence and critically analysing it, acquitted the accused-opposite party from all the charges framed against him and he was set at liberty vide impugned judgment and order dated 18.03.2023.

12. Aggrieved by the said judgment and order, the instant Government Appeal under Section 378 (3)
Cr.P.C. on behalf of the State/appellant has been preferred along with an application for leave to appeal.

13. Learned State Counsel relying upon the prosecution witnesses has submitted that the trial court has failed to appreciate the evidence in its true perspective and acquitted the accused-opposite party by wrong appreciation of the evidence available on record.
He has further submitted that the findings recorded by the trial court in the impugned judgment and order are perverse, illegal and bad in law warranting interference by this Court.

14. Since this appeal is against the acquittal, it will be relevant to note the principles of law laid down by the Apex Court with regard to the appreciation of evidence and approach to be adopted while dealing with an appeal against acquittal.
15. In Jafarudheen and others vs. State of Kerala, 2022 SCC Online SC 495, reiterating the principle on the subject the Hon'ble Apex Court reminded to the Courts as extracted below:

entities.text: Jafarudheen and others vs. State of Kerala, 2022 SCC Online SC 495
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: "25. While dealing with an appeal against acquittal by invoking Section 378 of the Cr.PC, the Appellate Court has to consider whether the Trial Court's view can be termed as a possible one, particularly when evidence on record has been analyzed.

sentences.text: 3 The reason is that an order of acquittal adds up to the presumption of innocence in favour of the accused.
Thus, the Appellate Court has to be relatively slow in reversing the order of the Trial Court rendering acquittal.
Therefore, the presumption in favour of the accused does not get weakened but only strengthened.

Such a double presumption that enures in favour of the accused has to be disturbed only by thorough scrutiny on the accepted legal parameters."
16.

In Mohan alias Srinivas alias Seena alias Tailor Seena vs. State of Karnataka, (2022) 12 SCC 619,
the Hon'ble Apex Court held as hereunder:
"20. Section 378 CrPC enables the State to prefer an appeal against an order of acquittal Section 384 CrPC speaks of the powers that can be exercised by the Appellate Court.

entities.text: Mohan alias Srinivas alias Seena alias Tailor Seena vs. State of Karnataka, (2022) 12 SCC 619
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
When the trial court renders its decision by acquitting the accused,
presumption of innocence gathers strength before the Appellate Court.
As a consequence, the onus on the prosecution becomes more burdensome as there is a double presumption of innocence.

Certainly, the Court of first instance has its own advantages in delivering its verdict, which is to see the witnesses in person while they depose The Appellate Court is expected to involve itself in a deeper, studied scrutiny of not only the evidence before it, but is duty bound to satisfy itself whether the decision of the trial court is both possible and plausible view
When two views are possible, the one taken by the trial court in a case of acquittal is to be followed on the touchstone of liberty along with the advantage of having seen the witnesses.

Article 21 of the Constitution of India also aids the accused after acquittal in a certain way,
though not absolute.
Suffice it is to state that the Appellate Court shall remind itself of the role required to play, while dealing with a case of an acquittal.

17. In Atley v. State of U.P., 1955 Cri. LJ 1653, the approach of the appellate court while considering a judgment of acquittal was discussed and it was observed that unless the appellate court comes to the conclusion that the judgment of the acquittal was perverse, it could not set aside the same.
18.

entities.text: Atley v. State of U.P., 1955 Cri. LJ 1653
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
The Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Bannareddy v. State of Karnataka, (2018) 5 SCC 790, has considered the power and jurisdiction of the High Court while interfering in an appeal against acquittal and held as under:
"26. The High Court should not have re-appreciated the evidence in its entirety,
especially when there existed no grave infirmity in the findings of the trial Court.

entities.text: Bannareddy v. State of Karnataka, (2018) 5 SCC 790
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: There exists no justification behind setting aside the order of acquittal passed by the trial Court, especially when the prosecution case suffers from several contradictions and infirmities".

19. In Ramesh Babulal Doshi vs. State of Gujarat, (1996) 9 SCC 225, the Hon'ble Apex Court observed vis-a-vis the powers of an appellate court while dealing with a judgment of acquittal and held like this :

sentences.text: While sitting in judgment over an acquittal the appellate court is first required to seek an answer to the question whether the findings of the trial court are palpably wrong, manifestly erroneous or demonstrably unsustainable.
If the appellate court answers the above question in the negative the order of acquittal is not to be disturbed.

Conversely, if the appellate court holds, for reasons to be recorded, that the order of acquittal cannot at all be sustained in view of any of the above infirmities it can then and then only reappraise the evidence to arrive at its own conclusions."

20. In the light of the submissions made by learned counsel for both the sides, we have carefully gone through the evidence available on record, its analysis and appreciation thereof and conclusion arrived at by the trial court in the impugned judgment and order dated 18.03.2023.
21.
The genesis of the prosecution story is that the victim was a minor girl aged about 14 years and she with his brother used to live along with the accused-opposite party, who was his father.
Taking advantage of the said situation, accused-opposite party was committing rape upon her by putting her under fear of death.

On 25.06.2017 at about 04:00 p.m., while she was all alone in the house,
accused-opposite party caught hold of her and committed rape upon her on the gun point.
On her raising alarm, his brother reached there and resisted his conduct and asked his father not to do so.

Then, the accused-opposite party started hurling abuses to them and with an intention to kill them,
assaulted them with the butt of the country made pistol causing injuries to them.
On their raising alarm number of villagers reached there and rescued the children, who thereafter reached at their maternal uncle's house and the FIR was lodged.
22. The learned trial court proceeded to scrutinize the evidence on record to find out the truth behind the prosecution story.

The prosecution mainly relied upon the testimony of P.W.2 the prosecutrix, who in her testimony has stated that on 25.06.2017 at about 04:00 p.m., she was at her father's house where her brother also used to reside.

On the day of incident, while she along with her brother was present in the house at about 04:00 p.m., his father came in her room and called her and thereafter undressed her and also undressed himself and committed rape upon her.

On raising alarm, her brother Akash also reached there and asked him to refrain from such conduct, however,
he paid no heed consequently, she along with his brother reached at his maternal uncle's house and since then is residing with her maternal uncle.
23. She further stated that after about five days of the said incident i.e. on 30.06.2017, her father came at her maternal uncle's house and forcibly tried to take her away, however, she refused.
Thereafter, she disclosed the entire incident to her maternal aunt, who narrated the incident to her husband (first informant) and he thereafter lodged the report.
Her statements under Section 161 and 164 Cr.P.C. were recorded, which has been proved.
She further categorically stated in her examination-in-chief that the incident of rape was witnessed by her brother.
24. During cross-examination before the Magistrate, she is stated to have disclosed the correct facts.
She, in her cross-examination, has stated that her father used to run the shop of Bisaatkhana and also work as an electrician.

She further categorically stated that because of electrocution one of his hand had become functionless to the extent that it could not open due to which he used to do his State Of Up vs Karn Singh S/O Nakliram on 7 February, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/62907323/
5 work only by one hand and on account of electrocution, he remained on bed for six months.

26. It is germane to point out here that the maternal aunt of the prosecutrix has not been examined and only his maternal uncle has been examined as P.W.1, whose testimony is certainly based on hearsay evidence.

sentences.text: 28. P.W.4 S.S.I. Satish Kumar is the second Investigating Officer, who conducted the investigation and submitted the charge-sheet against the accused-opposite party.
P.W.5 Anuj Shekhar produced the school admission register of the victim and proved her age.

29. P.W.6 is the brother of the victim and he, in his testimony, has not supported the prosecution story at all but merely stated that on the day of incident, he along with his sister was beaten by his father and hurled abused.
He further denied to have given any statement to the police.

At this stage,
he was declared hostile and was cross-examined by the prosecution.

During cross-examination, on his attention being drawn to his statement shown to be recorded under Section 161 Cr.P.C., he categorically denied to have given any such statement to the police and showed his ignorance as to how such statement was recorded.

30. During cross-examination, P.W.6 further stated that on account of electrocution, one of his father's hand had become functionless and he was granted a sum of Rs.5,00,000/- as compensation,
which was kept by his maternal uncle and when he denied to return the said money, there was a quarrel between the two and his father was beaten and thereafter his maternal uncle in league with his sister had lodged the instant case against his father.

31. From the careful perusal of the impugned judgment, we find that the trial court examined all the relevant aspects of the matter and has critically thrashed the entire evidence on record and it has been found that the incident in question had taken place on 25.06.2017, however, the FIR has been lodged only on 30.06.2017, after four days of the incident and the delay in lodging the FIR has not been explained at all, which creates a serious dent in the prosecution story.

32. Further, when we go through the entire evidence, we find that the prosecution story is primarily based on the testimonies of P.W.2, the prosecutrix herself and the statement of P.W.6, brother of the victim, who had not supported the prosecution story and thus, we find that the prosecution story is mainly based upon the sole testimony of the prosecutrix.
33. When we go through the testimony of P.W.2, we find that there are several contradictions in her testimony.
The testimony of the prosecutrix as narrated in the testimony before the court is in complete contradiction to her statement recorded under Section 164 Cr.P.C..

To be precise, the manner in which the incident is said to have been committed, as narrated in the statement of the prosecutrix under Section 164 Cr.P.C., is in complete contradiction to her statement recorded before the trial court.
34. In her statement under Section 164 Cr.P.C., the incident is said to have taken place on two consecutive days.

On the first day of incident, it is stated that only an attempt to rape her was made and on alarm being raised her brother reached there and rescued her, consequent to which, he was severely beaten by the accused-opposite party and thereafter he ran away to his maternal uncle's house and on the next day, the accused-opposite party again committed rape upon her and severely beaten her.

On resistance and alarm being raised by her, her neighbours reached at the place of State Of Up vs Karn Singh S/O Nakliram on 7 February, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/62907323/
7 incident and rescued her.

35. Thus, we find that the manner of incident, as narrated by P.W.2 in her statement under Section 164 Cr.P.C., is in sharp contradiction to the manner of the incident as narrated in her testimony before the court, wherein she has categorically stated that the incident took place on 25.06.2017,
when she was subjected to rape.
This particular circumstance clinchingly raises a serious dent in the prosecution story and makes the testimony of P.W.2 highly doubtful.

Further analyzing the evidence of P.W.2, we find that she in her cross-examination has categorically stated:

Thus, from the said testimony, we find that the testimony of the victim is, in fact, a tutored one and is not her natural statement, which further creates a serious dent in the prosecution story and makes her testimony doubtful.
Furthermore, when we go through the testimony of P.W.2, we find that the manner in which the incident is said to have been committed by the accused-opposite party does not inspire confidence.

She in her statement has categorically stated that:

37.
If we analyze the said testimony of the witness, we find that statement of the prosecutrix does not inspire confidence.

The manner in which the incident is said to have taken place is evident from the aforesaid testimony, discussed above, however, we find that her statement is unnatural and do not inspire our confidence in the manner as alleged.
38. Admittedly, it is the specific case of the prosecution that she was severely beaten by the accused-opposite party, however, the doctor has not found any injury on her person.

Furthermore,
when we analyze the testimony of P.W.6, the brother of the victim, in light of the statement of P.W.2, we find that though she has admitted the presence of P.W.6 at the time of incident, who is said to have rescued her but in his testimony, her brother has completely denied the prosecution story and has submitted that since there was a dispute between his maternal uncle and his father over return of the compensation money, his father has been falsely implicated.
He further stated that on the day of incident, he along with her sister was merely beaten by his father and no further incident had taken place.

39. Thus, we find that the testimony of P.W.6 is in sharp contradiction to the statement of P.W.2.

8 inspire confidence and she cannot be said to be a witness of sterling quality.

sentences.text: 40. It is further germane to point out here that the trial court in its judgment has vividly discussed the entire testimony of the witnesses and has reached a just conclusion that the prosecution has failed to prove its case against the accused-opposite party and has rightly acquitted him.

This Court also finds that although the instant case is a case under POCSO Act, wherein a presumption of guilt of the accused may be drawn, but since in the instant case, the evidence on record is very shaky and the testimony of P.W.2 cannot be said to be of sterling quality, as such, it does not inspire confidence and the conviction cannot be based on the shaky testimony of the prosecutrix.

41. There are several major lacunas in the prosecution story and evidence as well, as such, the presumption of innocence on the part of the accused-opposite party certainly arise and the case is pulled out of the purview of the POCSO Act.

42. It is notable that in the sexual offence case, the evidence of the prosecutrix has got a distinguished place, which must be paid respect to but since the same does not inspire our confidence and is not a reliable witness and consistent, the trial court was never bound to act upon the testimony of such an unreliable witness.

43. In Mohd. Ali @ Guddu vs. State of Uttar Pradesh, (2015) 7 Supreme Court Cases 272, it has been held by the Hon'ble Apex Court that there can be no iota of doubt that a conviction can be based upon sole testimony of prosecutrix, even without corroboration, if it is unimpeachable and beyond reproach.

entities.text: Mohd. Ali @ Guddu vs. State of Uttar Pradesh, (2015) 7 Supreme Court Cases 272
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
In the said case considering the entire circumstances of the case and particularly the testimony of the prosecutrix, it was found that it leave a mark of doubt to treat the testimony of the prosecutrix as so natural and truthful to inspire confidence and it was concluded that the evidence of prosecutrix was not of such quality which can be placed reliance.
44.

The prosecutrix, in the case in hand, is a witness not falling into the category of 'sterling witness'
hence, in our considered opinion, it was not safe for the learned trial court to rely upon the sole testimony of the prosecutrix.

45. It is settled legal position that in acquittal appeals, the appellate Court is not required to rewrite the judgment or to give fresh reasoning, when the reasons assigned by the trial Court are found to be just and proper.

46. In the case of State of Karnataka vs. Hemareddy, AIR 1981, SC 1417, it has been held by the Hon'ble Apex Court as under :
" ...

The Hon'ble Apex Court in Shivasharanappa and others vs. State of Karnataka, JT 2013 (7) SC 66 has held as under:
"That appellate Court is empowered to reappreciate the entire evidence, though,
certain other principles are also to be adhered to and it has to be kept in mind that acquittal results into double presumption of innocence."
48.

The Apex Court in Shailendra Rajdev Pasvan v. State of Gujarat, (2020) 14 SC 750, has held that if the appellate court is reversing the trial court's order of acquittal, it should give proper weight and consideration to the presumption of innocence in favour of accused, and to the principle that such a presumption sands reinforced, reaffirmed and strengthened by the trial court and in Samsul Haque v. State of Assam, (2019) 18 SCC 161 held that the judgment of acquittal, where two views are possible, should not be set aside, even if view formed by appellate court may be a more probable one, interference with acquittal can only be justified when it is based on a perverse view.
49.

sentences.text: In view of the aforesaid discussions, we are of the view that the learned trial Court has given logical and plausible findings in the impugned judgment and has rightly concluded that the prosecution has miserably failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt.

The judgment and order of the trial court under judicious scrutiny is just and proper and carries no perversity therein, hence,
it does not warrant any interference by this Court.
The reasoning adopted by the learned Trial Judge is based upon proper application of judicial mind.
No illegality or infirmity is found in the impugned judgment and order and it needs no interference by this Court.
50. In view of the foregoing discussions, we are of the opinion that the application for leave to appeal filed by the State has no force and it is, accordingly, dismissed.
Consequent thereto, the instant Government Appeal also stands dismissed.

51. Let a copy of this judgment and order be forwarded to the court concerned alongwith trial court record for information and necessary compliance.

opennyai_summary.arguments:
13. Learned State Counsel relying upon the prosecution witnesses has submitted that the trial court has failed to appreciate the evidence in its true perspective and acquitted the accused-opposite party by wrong appreciation of the evidence available on record.
He has further submitted that the findings recorded by the trial court in the impugned judgment and order are perverse, illegal and bad in law warranting interference by this Court.
opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
14. Since this appeal is against the acquittal, it will be relevant to note the principles of law laid down by the Apex Court with regard to the appreciation of evidence and approach to be adopted while dealing with an appeal against acquittal.
In Mohan alias Srinivas alias Seena alias Tailor Seena vs. State of Karnataka, (2022) 12 SCC 619,
the Hon'ble Apex Court held as hereunder:
"20. Section 378 CrPC enables the State to prefer an appeal against an order of acquittal Section 384 CrPC speaks of the powers that can be exercised by the Appellate Court.
Certainly, the Court of first instance has its own advantages in delivering its verdict, which is to see the witnesses in person while they depose The Appellate Court is expected to involve itself in a deeper, studied scrutiny of not only the evidence before it, but is duty bound to satisfy itself whether the decision of the trial court is both possible and plausible view
When two views are possible, the one taken by the trial court in a case of acquittal is to be followed on the touchstone of liberty along with the advantage of having seen the witnesses.
Article 21 of the Constitution of India also aids the accused after acquittal in a certain way,
though not absolute.
Suffice it is to state that the Appellate Court shall remind itself of the role required to play, while dealing with a case of an acquittal.
The Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Bannareddy v. State of Karnataka, (2018) 5 SCC 790, has considered the power and jurisdiction of the High Court while interfering in an appeal against acquittal and held as under:
"26. The High Court should not have re-appreciated the evidence in its entirety,
especially when there existed no grave infirmity in the findings of the trial Court.
This Court also finds that although the instant case is a case under POCSO Act, wherein a presumption of guilt of the accused may be drawn, but since in the instant case, the evidence on record is very shaky and the testimony of P.W.2 cannot be said to be of sterling quality, as such, it does not inspire confidence and the conviction cannot be based on the shaky testimony of the prosecutrix.
The prosecutrix, in the case in hand, is a witness not falling into the category of 'sterling witness'
hence, in our considered opinion, it was not safe for the learned trial court to rely upon the sole testimony of the prosecutrix.
45. It is settled legal position that in acquittal appeals, the appellate Court is not required to rewrite the judgment or to give fresh reasoning, when the reasons assigned by the trial Court are found to be just and proper.
The Apex Court in Shailendra Rajdev Pasvan v. State of Gujarat, (2020) 14 SC 750, has held that if the appellate court is reversing the trial court's order of acquittal, it should give proper weight and consideration to the presumption of innocence in favour of accused, and to the principle that such a presumption sands reinforced, reaffirmed and strengthened by the trial court and in Samsul Haque v. State of Assam, (2019) 18 SCC 161 held that the judgment of acquittal, where two views are possible, should not be set aside, even if view formed by appellate court may be a more probable one, interference with acquittal can only be justified when it is based on a perverse view.
49.
In view of the aforesaid discussions, we are of the view that the learned trial Court has given logical and plausible findings in the impugned judgment and has rightly concluded that the prosecution has miserably failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt.
The judgment and order of the trial court under judicious scrutiny is just and proper and carries no perversity therein, hence,
it does not warrant any interference by this Court.
The reasoning adopted by the learned Trial Judge is based upon proper application of judicial mind.
No illegality or infirmity is found in the impugned judgment and order and it needs no interference by this Court.
opennyai_summary.decision:
50. In view of the foregoing discussions, we are of the opinion that the application for leave to appeal filed by the State has no force and it is, accordingly, dismissed.
Consequent thereto, the instant Government Appeal also stands dismissed.
